title: State v. Albaidhani
description: Whether law enforcement officers qualify as "victims" under Marsy's Law and are entitled to have their names redacted from public filings.
plaintiff_argument: Officers One and Two argued that they qualify as victims under Marsy's Law and are entitled to have their names and identifying information redacted from public filings to prevent harassment.
defendant_argument: Samir Albaidhani argued that Marsy's Law does not apply to law enforcement officers and that redacting names would violate his constitutional rights, including the right to confront accusers, and that there is no victim until a conviction.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the circuit court's decision, holding that law enforcement officers can be victims under Marsy's Law and their names/initials can be redacted from public filings if they could be used to locate or harass them, remanding the case for a balancing test of the victims' rights against the defendant's and public's rights.

title: In re: Lieutenant Governor’s Power to Vote on Final Passage of Legislation
description: Whether the South Dakota Constitution grants the Lieutenant Governor the authority to cast a tie-breaking vote on the final passage of a bill or joint resolution while serving as President of the Senate.
plaintiff_argument: The Governor sought an advisory opinion, implicitly arguing that the Lieutenant Governor has the constitutional authority to cast a tie-breaking vote on the final passage of legislation.
defendant_argument: The Senate Leadership argued that the Lieutenant Governor does not have the authority to cast a tie-breaking vote on the final passage of legislation, contending that only elected members should vote on final passage and that the court should not intervene in the Senate's internal affairs.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the South Dakota Constitution empowers the Lieutenant Governor, while serving as President of the Senate, to cast a tie-breaking vote in the Senate on any matter, including the final passage of a bill.

title: Gonzales v. Markland
description: Whether the jury district used for Donika Rae Gonzales' trial violated her constitutional right to a trial by an impartial jury from a fair cross-section of the community, or if her counsel was ineffective.
plaintiff_argument: Gonzales argued that the jury district unconstitutionally diluted the percentage of prospective Native American jurors and that her counsel was ineffective for failing to object to the jury composition and not explaining its ramifications.
defendant_argument: Markland argued that the habeas court erred in its interpretation of the United States and South Dakota Constitutions, its application of the Duren test, and its conclusion that the alleged errors constituted structural error, asserting that the jury district was constitutional and Gonzales' rights were not violated.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the habeas court's judgment, vacating the order that granted habeas relief and upholding Gonzales' conviction.

title: State v. Waldner
description: Whether the circuit court erred by requiring E.H. to produce her diaries and journals, considering her right to privacy under Marsy's Law versus the defendants' right to a fair trial and the subpoena's compliance with the Nixon factors.
plaintiff_argument: E.H. argued that the subpoena violated her constitutional right to privacy and her right to refuse discovery requests under Marsy's Law, and that she did not waive these rights. She also contended the subpoena failed to meet the relevancy, admissibility, and specificity requirements of the Nixon test.
defendant_argument: The Waldners argued their constitutional right to a fair trial outweighed E.H.'s right to privacy, asserting that E.H. waived her privacy rights by disclosing one journal and that the requested journals were relevant to E.H.'s credibility.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the circuit court's order denying E.H.'s motion to quash the subpoena and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: In re Noem
description: Whether Article III, § 12 of the South Dakota Constitution prohibits all contracts between legislators and the State, with the plaintiff arguing for a broader prohibition including contracts funded by general appropriations, and the defendant arguing for a narrower prohibition limited to contracts authorized by specific legislation.
plaintiff_argument: Governor Noem sought clarification on whether various legislator interests in state contracts violate Article III, § 12, suggesting that some interests might be too indirect to fall under the prohibition, and that general appropriation bills might not authorize specific contracts.
defendant_argument: The Legislature argued that Article III, § 12 only prohibits contracts specifically 'authorized' by law during a legislator's term, not those merely funded by general appropriation bills, and asked the court to overrule precedent that held otherwise.
decision_outcome: The court overruled its prior decisions in Asphalt Surfacing and Pitts, holding that Article III, § 12 does not prohibit all contracts between legislators and the State, but only those authorized by specific laws passed during a legislator's term, clarifying that general appropriation legislation only allocates funds and does not authorize specific contracts.

title: In re: Legislator Interest in State Contracts
description: Whether Article III, § 12 of the South Dakota Constitution prohibits all contracts between legislators and the State, specifically concerning contracts authorized by general appropriation bills.
plaintiff_argument: The Governor sought clarity on Article III, § 12, suggesting that a legislator's interest in a state contract might be too indirect to violate the provision, even if funded by a general appropriation bill.
defendant_argument: The Legislature argued that general appropriation bills do not "authorize" specific contracts in the way Article III, § 12 intends, and that prior rulings (Asphalt Surfacing) incorrectly broadened the prohibition, asking the court to overrule them.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that Article III, § 12 does not prohibit all contracts between legislators and the State, specifically stating that general appropriation legislation only allocates money and does not authorize specific contracts for ordinary expenses, thereby overruling Asphalt Surfacing and Pitts.

title: Thom v. Barnett (In re Election Contest Dakota Constitution to Legalize)
description: Whether Initiated Constitutional Amendment A, which legalizes, regulates, and taxes marijuana and mandates legislation for medical marijuana and hemp, violates the single-subject rule of the South Dakota Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that Amendment A violated Article XXIII, § 1 of the South Dakota Constitution by embracing multiple distinct subjects and was a constitutional revision requiring a convention under Article XXIII, § 2.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that Amendment A complied with Article XXIII, § 1 and § 2, as it pertained to no more than one subject and amended rather than revised the Constitution.
decision_outcome: The South Dakota Supreme Court affirmed the circuit court's decision that Initiated Constitutional Amendment A violated the single-subject rule of the South Dakota Constitution and was therefore void in its entirety.

title: Hamen v. Hamlin County
description: Whether law enforcement's damage to private property during the arrest of an alleged fleeing felon constitutes a compensable taking under the state constitution or a violation of federal constitutional rights under 42 U.S.C. § 1983.
plaintiff_argument: The Hamens argued they were entitled to compensation for property damage under the state constitution's damages clause (inverse condemnation) and that the Sheriff violated their Fourth and Fourteenth Amendment rights under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 through unlawful entry and excessive force.
defendant_argument: The Sheriff argued his actions were an exercise of police power, not a compensable taking, and that he was entitled to qualified immunity for the § 1983 claims because no constitutional violations occurred or were clearly established.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court dismissed the inverse condemnation claim and the excessive force claim, but allowed the unlawful entry claim to proceed to trial.
